claims.text: Single-phase solid-solution formation in noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles is primarily governed by atomic-interdiffusion kinetics controlled by transient liquid-phase formation.
Heating rate and a brief hold near peak temperature set the timescale for fission/fusion events that homogenize the elemental distribution before quenching.
Deviation from an optimal thermal profile causes insufficient interdiffusion and promotes phase separation or elemental segregation.
A representative rapid-synthesis baseline uses approximately 55 ms of heating at 2000 K in argon followed by cooling at about 10^5 K/s on carbon supports.
Rapid heating and cooling can produce a single solid-solution HEA nanoparticle state by suppressing secondary-phase formation.
The rapid-heating baseline is often prone to phase separation, compositional imperfections, and morphological defects.
Slightly reducing the heating rate or adding a short near-peak hold will extend the period of transient liquid-phase formation.
Extending the transient liquid period will enhance atomic interdiffusion before quenching.
The proposed intervention applies to systems containing more than five noble-metal elements processed near 2000 K under inert atmosphere with rapid cooling.
Carbon-based or similar supports provide sufficiently uniform heating for the proposed mechanism.
A transient liquid phase forms at high temperature in the targeted noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles.
The transient liquid phase mediates fission/fusion and atomic mixing between the precursor state and the final quenched solid solution.
A moderated thermal profile prolongs the transient liquid state and permits more complete interdiffusion.
An overly brief liquid state causes differential elemental diffusion, phase separation, and secondary-phase formation.
A controlled thermal ramp enables short-range ordering that favors a uniform high-entropy phase.
Relative to the rapid-heating baseline, moderated heating will improve compositional homogeneity and reduce elemental segregation and secondary phases.
Moderated heating will reduce uncontrolled nanoparticle morphology relative to the baseline.
The hypothesis is limited to high-temperature noble metal–based HEAs with closely spaced melting points.
Systems lacking a transient liquid phase or processed under substantially slower cooling may be governed by other formation mechanisms.
The optimal heating-rate reduction or hold duration depends on composition and remains unquantified.
